How do I feel? Um, honestly, it's just this massive wave of panic. And guilt, just so much guilt. Like, the minute I finally stop eating, the reality of what I just did hits me like a ton of bricks. My stomach is physically hurting because it's so stretched out, and I'm just standing there looking at the empty wrappers and the dirty plates, and my heart starts racing. 

And because I know how digestion works—you know, with my biology background and everything—my brain immediately goes into overdrive about absorption. I just start thinking, I have to get this out. I have to undo this right now. So... I almost always end up rushing to the bathroom. I lock the door, even though I live completely alone, which is stupid, I know, but I do it anyway. And I just... I make myself throw up. 

It's just, it feels like the absolute only way to fix what I just broke. If I don't do it, the panic just keeps building and building until I feel like I'm going to jump out of my skin. I just have to get it out before the calories have a chance to settle in and actually absorb into my body. And then after I do that, after I throw up, there's this weird, brief moment of relief, like I hit a reset button. But then the shame comes right back, and I'm just sitting on the bathroom tiles, rinsing my mouth out, looking in the mirror and wondering how I let it happen again. It's just this whole exhausting cycle, and I hate it, I really do, but in that moment right after I eat, the urge to just purge it all is so overwhelming I can't even think straight until it's done.

Underweight? Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, I'm definitely not underweight. If anything, I'm probably right in the middle, maybe even a little heavier than I'd like to be, honestly. It's funny you ask that because, with my biology background, I actually pay a lot of attention to BMI and weight distribution and all that stuff, probably more than I should. But my weight... it fluctuates a bit, but it never drops down into what anyone would call underweight. It's actually one of the things that makes me feel so crazy about this whole cycle. Like, I'm eating thousands of calories in a single sitting, and then I'm throwing it all up, but my body just kind of stays the same. Or at least, it doesn't change enough for anyone else to notice. Exercise excessively? Um, no, not really. I mean, honestly, by the time I get home from the sanctuary, the thought of going for a run or hitting the gym is just... it's completely laughable. Like I was saying before, my job is already so intensely physical. I spend eight, sometimes ten or twelve hours a day on my feet, moving non-stop. So by the time I actually walk through my front door at night, my muscles are already aching, my back is sore, and I'm just completely, utterly drained. The physical labor is basically my workout, and it's a pretty intense one. 

So when these... these eating episodes happen, which is usually late at night when I'm already running on empty, I don't try to sweat it out. I don't hop on a treadmill or do jumping jacks or anything like that. The panic hits, and my immediate reaction is just to get it out the absolute fastest way possible, which is... well, throwing up in the bathroom, like I mentioned. I don't even think I'd have the physical energy to exercise it off even if I wanted to, because the binge itself kind of makes me feel so heavy and sluggish, and my body is already so battered from working with the animals all day. So, no, I don't do the whole excessive exercise thing. The purging is... it's the only thing I do to try and fix it.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Laxatives? Or diuretics? Um, no. No, I've never really gone down that route. Honestly, with my biology background, I just... I think too much about the human digestive tract and how long things actually take to process. Like, if you take a laxative, the food has already been sitting in your stomach, it's already moving through the small intestine, so the nutrients and, well, the massive amount of calories are already being absorbed into your bloodstream. So in my head, it just doesn't make any logical sense to use them if the whole goal is to get rid of what I just binged on. 

Plus, practically speaking, with my job at the sanctuary, I absolutely cannot afford to have, you know, unpredictable stomach issues or dehydration the next day. Imagine trying to clean out a massive, muddy enclosure or trying to wrangle a terrified, fifty-pound rescue dog while worrying about needing to sprint to the restroom because you took a laxative the night before. Or being dizzy from diuretics while carrying heavy feed bags. It would be a complete disaster, and it wouldn't be fair to the animals either. They need me present and focused. 

So, no, I stay away from those completely. For me, it's just... well, like I was saying before, after I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up because it feels like the only way to undo it before the calories settle in. It's all about the immediacy of it, you know? The panic hits the absolute second I swallow that last bite of whatever I'm eating, and I just have this overwhelming, suffocating sensation that I need to hit the reset button right that very second. If I wait, if I just let all that food sit there in my stomach, I can almost physically feel my body starting to break it down, and that thought just completely terrifies me. So throwing up is... it's immediate. It's really the only thing that gives me that instant, albeit temporary, relief. It gives me that false sense that I've somehow erased the whole mistake before it becomes a permanent part of me, without having to wait hours for a pill to kick in.

Oh, God, yes. It's... honestly, it's terrifying. It's not just when I binge, either, it's this constant, looming dread that just hangs over me all the time. Like, I have this routine where I'll check my weight, usually right after a long shift at the sanctuary, when I'm already exhausted and covered in dirt and hay. I just can't stand the thought of it. The panic of feeling my clothes not fit exactly the way they did yesterday is just so overwhelming, I can't focus on anything else until I figure out a plan to fix it.

Emotionally? Um... wow, I don't... I don't really know if I have a clear answer for that. It's this horrible, loud spiral in my head of \"you're losing control, you're getting soft, you're letting yourself go.\" And then, almost automatically, I start planning how to make up for it. I'll be calculating in my head while I'm working, thinking, \"Okay, I have to skip lunch today, I'll just drink black coffee, I'll take on the extra heavy lifting with the feed bags to burn more, I won't eat anything until tomorrow night.\" \n\nIt just consumes my thoughts completely. Because in my head, gaining weight means I'm failing, you know? It means all that intense physical labor I do isn't enough, and it just... it drives me crazy. I just can't stand the thought of it. The panic of feeling my clothes not fit exactly the way they did yesterday is just so overwhelming, I can't focus on anything else until I figure out a plan to fix it.\n\nDoctor: How are you feeling emotionally right before one of these binge eating episodes starts?\n\nPatient: Emotionally? Um... wow, I don't... I don't really know if I have a clear answer for that. Like, if you're asking if I'm sitting there feeling super sad, or angry, or, I don't know, crying about something? It's really not like that at all. I think people always assume there's this big emotional trigger, you know? Like on TV where someone has a horrible day or gets dumped and they just start eating everything in sight. But for me... I honestly haven't noticed feeling much of anything right before it starts. Emotionally, I mean. \n\nPhysically, like I was saying before, I'm just completely drained from the sanctuary, my muscles are aching from the feed bags, I'm covered in dirt, but emotionally? It's almost like my brain is just... blank. It's like a void. I'm not stressed about the animals, I'm not upset about my life, I'm just... numb, I guess? But not numb in a depressed way, just... switched off. Like I'm on autopilot. I'll be walking through the front door, dropping my keys on the counter, taking off my boots, and I'm not thinking about my feelings at all. \n\nThe emotional part—the absolute panic, the suffocating anxiety I was telling you about—that doesn't hit until *after* I've eaten, when the reality of what I've just done sets in. But leading up to it? Right before I take that first bite of whatever it is? I really couldn't tell you. There's no specific mood or feeling that I can pinpoint. It's just this strange absence of emotion, just a total blank slate until the switch flips and I'm already eating.\n\nDoctor: Is your fear of gaining weight the main reason you purge after binge eating?\n\nPatient: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. It's... well, it's entirely about that. When I'm sitting there, right after the binge is over, and I'm just looking at the empty boxes or the wrappers, that's when the reality of it just completely crashes down on me. I start thinking about all the food I just consumed. Like, thousands of calories, just sitting there in my stomach like a lead weight. And my brain just goes into this absolute panic mode, picturing all of it turning into fat, making those heavy canvas work pants I told you about even tighter, basically undoing all the intense physical labor I did at the sanctuary all day. \n\nIt's like a ticking clock in my head. I'll be sitting there, feeling so incredibly full, like physically in pain from how much I ate, and my brain is just screaming at me that I only have a very small window of time to fix this. So, after I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up because it feels like the only way to undo it before the calories settle in. \n\nI just have this terrifying image of my body absorbing all of it, and if I don't get it out right then and there, if I let it digest, then I've permanently ruined everything. And it's awful, it really is an awful thing to have to do, but in that moment, it's the only thing that gives me any relief from that absolute terror of gaining weight. It's like I'm hitting a reset button, or at least I try to convince myself I am. Because the alternative—just sitting there on the couch and letting my body process all that food—is just completely unthinkable to me. I would probably lose my mind just sitting there waiting for it to turn into weight. So, yeah, it's entirely about stopping those calories from settling in and changing my body.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're losing control when you start eating during these episodes?\n\nPatient: Yeah. Yeah, absolutely. It's... it's exactly like that. It's actually the main reason I finally decided to come in and talk to someone, because it's just getting so out of hand. Like I was saying, I get home from the sanctuary, and usually it's late, right? The sun is down, the house is completely quiet, I'm totally alone. And I'll just start eating. And it's not like I sit down and think, \"I'm going to eat all of this.\" It starts with just one thing. But then... it's like a switch flips in my brain, or like something else completely takes over my body. \n\nIt's the most bizarre, terrifying feeling. I'll be standing there in the kitchen, usually just in front of the open fridge or the pantry, not even bothering to put things on a plate half the time. And I'll be physically reaching for more food, shoving it in my mouth, and in my head, I'm screaming at myself. My inner monologue is literally going, \"Stop, what are you doing? Put it away, close the door, just walk out of the kitchen, go to bed.\" I am fully aware that I shouldn't be doing it, and I'm actively telling myself to stop, but my hands just won't listen. \n\nIt's like I'm a passenger in my own body. I'll just keep eating and eating, opening another box, unwrapping another thing, and I literally cannot force myself to stop until I'm so physically stuffed that it hurts, or until there's just nothing left that I want to eat. The disconnect between what my brain is telling me to do—which is to stop immediately—and what my body is actually doing is just... it's horrible. It makes me feel completely crazy. So, yeah, losing control doesn't even begin to cover it. It feels like I'm totally hijacked.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever try to burn off the calories from your binge eating episodes through excessive exercise?\n\nPatient: Excessive exercise? No, not really. I mean, I guess it depends on how you define exercise, right? Because, like I was telling you, my whole day is essentially one long, grueling workout. Being an animal caretaker, especially at a large sanctuary, it's not like sitting at a desk. I'm up at dawn, and from the moment I get there, I'm moving. I'm hauling fifty-pound bags of feed across muddy fields, I'm mucking out stalls, I'm repairing fences, I'm wrangling animals that weigh ten times what I do. It's incredibly physical work, and by the time I get home, I'm just completely destroyed. My back aches, my knees hurt, my arms feel like they're made of lead. \n\nSo the idea of coming home, having one of those... episodes, and then going for a run or hitting a gym? It's just physically impossible for me. I barely have the energy to drag myself up the stairs to my bedroom, let alone jump on a treadmill. And honestly, even on my days off, I'm usually so exhausted from the work week that I just want to lay flat on the floor and not move a single muscle. \n\nSo, no, I don't try to exercise it off. That's why the throwing up thing is... well, it's the only option I feel like I have. Because I can't burn it off. There's just no gas left in the tank for that. If I had a desk job, maybe it would be different, maybe I'd be one of those people who runs ten miles after eating too much, but for me, the throwing up is the only way I can get rid of it without having to exert any more physical energy, because I just don't have any left to give.\n\nDoctor: Is your fear of gaining weight the primary reason you feel compelled to purge after binge eating?\n\nPatient: Yeah, like I was saying earlier, it really is the whole driving force behind it. I know we kind of just touched on this, but I honestly cannot overstate how much that fear just completely consumes my thoughts. It's not just a passing worry, it's... well, to give you an idea of how bad it gets, if I step on the scale after a long shift at the sanctuary—and I weigh myself constantly, probably way more than I should—but if that number is even just a single pound higher than I think it should be, or, God forbid, if I'm getting dressed in the morning and those heavy canvas work pants feel even slightly tighter around my waist... my entire day is just completely derailed. \n\nI will literally spend the whole day out there, whether I'm feeding the animals or mucking out the barns, just agonizing over it. I'll be sweating, working my hands to the bone, and my mind is just racing, obsessing over the fact that I'm letting myself get fat. It's like this loud, blaring alarm going off in my head that I cannot mute, no matter how distracted I try to get with my work. And right away, the second I feel that tightness in my pants or see that number on the scale, I start planning exactly how I'm going to make up for it. \n\nMy brain just starts calculating, you know? Figuring out how I can fix it, how I can get rid of anything I eat later, mapping out the whole evening just to ensure that one pound doesn't turn into two, or five, or ten. It's this constant, exhausting, never-ending loop. So when you ask if that fear is the primary reason I feel compelled to get rid of the food... yes, a hundred percent. Because living with that panic, that creeping, physical sensation that my clothes don't fit right and that my body is expanding... I just can't tolerate it. It dictates absolutely everything I do.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever fast or restrict your food intake after one of these binge eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Fasting? Um... no. No, I really don't do that. And it's not because I don't want to, believe me. The morning after one of those nights, the absolute last thing I want to do is put anything else in my stomach. The guilt is just... it's suffocating, and the idea of eating again makes my skin crawl. But practically speaking? I just can't. \n\nIt really goes back to what I was saying earlier about the sanctuary and how incredibly physical the job is. If I try to go to work on an empty stomach, especially after... you know, after throwing up the night before... I would literally pass out in the middle of a paddock. I mean, just the other week, we had this massive delivery of alfalfa bales, and I was out there in the heat, stacking them in the barn for three hours straight. If I hadn't eaten breakfast, I wouldn't have made it through the first twenty minutes. \n\nOr, you know, if I'm trying to corral one of the rescue horses—we have this one, a draft cross, huge guy, easily eighteen hundred pounds, and he can get pretty spooky with loud noises. You have to be completely alert, totally grounded, and physically ready to hold your own if he pulls back on the lead rope. You cannot be lightheaded or have your hands shaking because you decided to skip meals to make up for a binge. It's actually a safety hazard for me and for the animals if I'm not physically operating at a hundred percent. \n\nSo, no matter how much I hate myself the next morning, no matter how much my brain is screaming at me to just zip my mouth shut and not eat a single calorie for the next twenty-four hours, I force myself to eat. I'll have breakfast, usually oatmeal or eggs, something that will stick to my ribs and actually give me the energy to do my job. And then I'll eat lunch, too, usually with the rest of the crew in the breakroom, so I look completely normal to everyone else. \n\nIt's such a weird disconnect, honestly. Because during the day, I'm eating like a totally regular, healthy guy who just needs fuel for heavy manual labor. I don't restrict my food at all during the shift. I eat exactly what I need to survive the day and get the work done. It's only when the sun goes down and I'm back in that empty, quiet house that everything just... unravels again.
